utterances.text: When you're not aware of plans, you can't ask them.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Where you knew of the operations that were unfolding, that you were informed about by members of the VRS, did you ask the members of the BH army --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, it's clear the witness, if he says you can't ask them whether that's true or not. He didn't. That's the gist of the answer. The witness also could have said, I didn't ask them and then ... Please proceed. Under no circumstances did you ever ask for such plans?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, because we didn't know that they existed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, but sometimes you can ask for something --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- you are not sure that it does exist, but that asking for it also is instrumental to gaining knowledge of possible existence. But let's not deal with that. The witness never asked.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Let us now discuss your freedom of movement; that is to say, the freedom of movement of the DutchBat across the enclave of Srebrenica. Up until one point, your DutchBat members enjoyed the freedom of movement around the enclave; right?

utterances.speaker: EVERT RAVE [Resumed]
utterances.text: We had no freedom movement around the enclave, only inside the enclave.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: That was my question, yes. At one point, however, you were deprived of the freedom of movement throughout the enclave; is that right?

utterances.speaker: EVERT RAVE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what you mean. When, or when, or what?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, were you -- did you want to know whether there was no freedom of movement throughout the enclave or that the freedom of movement within the enclave was not complete?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Within the enclave.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Within the enclave. Was there a time when you were not able to freely move around within the enclave?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, there was a time. I think it was the end of January, the beginning of February, that a part in the west enclave of the enclave our freedom of movement was restricted.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You were no longer able to gain access to an area called the Bandera triangle; right?

utterances.speaker: EVERT RAVE [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, is there any dispute about the lack of freedom of movement, because we've heard a lot of evidence, even elicited by the Prosecution, that freedom of movement was not complete and that, especially in the Bandera triangle, that there was no access for the DutchBat.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: There really isn't, Mr. President. This is the same material that we've heard before. They were disallowed access, especially by Zulfo Tursunovic's units in the Bandera triangle.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, so there no dispute about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: No. In fact, there's no dispute about much of this. If there's any wish to make any agreements on the policy of the BiH, their attacks outside of the enclave, many of these things were also dealt with in the open statement. We pointed them out ourselves.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Lukic, so therefore there's no -- unless there's anything new you want to explore. We've heard this evidence a couple of times. There's no dispute about it, so let's use our time best.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'll move on. [Interpretation] Let us now look at 1D892. [In English] I just checked, but this is also the same area, so I will not continue with this document, since it's also Bandera triangle.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then please move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can we agree -- this is the question. Is it true that ... since you did not have access to the Bandera triangle --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, there's another good reason not to use the last document because the translation is not a translation of the same document. You have two different documents in the English and the B/C/S. So if you want to use it ever in the future, take care that the two are corresponding.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Is it correct that since you did not have access to the Bandera triangle area, you were not aware of the activities unfolding there? And I mean the activities undertaken by the BH army.

utterances.speaker: EVERT RAVE [Resumed]
utterances.text: When you're not there, you can't see anything, so we weren't aware what was going on over there.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: But there can be other sources other than physical presence. You are telling us that you weren't aware of what was happening in the Bandera triangle.

utterances.speaker: EVERT RAVE [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Is it also correct that an official decision was taken within UNPROFOR to agree to there being no patrols within the Bandera triangle? Is there such an agreement on the part of UNPROFOR?

utterances.speaker: EVERT RAVE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Speaking about UNPROFOR, I think you mean with the Dutch battalion?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [In English] DutchBat. [No interpretation].

utterances.speaker: EVERT RAVE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think there was an agreement, because all the time we tried to get in our patrols and to get access to the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Is it correct that the commander of the DutchBat ordered his troops not to patrol in that area?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What's the difference between this one and the previous question, Mr. Lukic?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The agreement might be in between maybe UNPROFOR and Muslim side and obviously there was an order. And to be more clear, I'll call 1D887 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: -- to the e-court. We need page 3. It's testimony of this witness in Tolimir case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then go to -- to -- to what -- because you are talking about an official decision was taken within UNPROFOR to agree -- unknown to agree with whom. It's all -- it lacks precision in your questions, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: That's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But let's then move to what you want to put to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes. We need page 3. It should correspond to page 6820 from transcript from Tolimir case. And we need lines 12 to 18. I quote: "Can you tell us, finally, who decided you should not patrol in the Bandera triangle? "A. Of course, I got my orders from the commander of the Dutch battalion in the enclave and it might be possible that he got the orders from commander UNPROFOR, but I really don't know. I know that finally the commander of DutchBat ordered his troops not to patrol in the area."

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Therefore, is it correct, and do you stand by this testimony in the Tolimir case, that the commander of the Dutch battalion ordered his troops not to patrol in the area of the Bandera triangle?

utterances.speaker: EVERT RAVE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think when I stated this in Tolimir case, of course, but you can also seen in line 18, "Although we tried it several times ..." And I don't know at what moment the order was given not to patrol there. And my opinion now is that we tried all the time to get access to that area, not only by patrolling there, and I don't know at what moment the commander of the Dutch battalion took the position not to go in.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: So does your statement that the commander of the Dutch battalion issued such an order to his troops still stand, or does it not stand anymore?

utterances.speaker: EVERT RAVE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah, in my opinion, it might be well possible that the commander ordered not to patrol in the area. But I don't know for how long, but it's possible, yes. I stay to this statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'm closing to an end, just to inform everybody. I'll just go through my documents and see if I have some -- any last questions. Give me one minute.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Only I want to inform Your Honours that we were informed by the Prosecution yesterday that this ultimatum we discussed yesterday was located among 65 ter Prosecutor's documents and it's 05751. So ... it's basically --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If the parties think it useful and to have it in evidence, because there have been several references to an ultimatum, then --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: At least we would propose.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could it be tendered from the bar table?

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The ultimatum. You can tender it from the bar table now if you wish or if you leave it to Mr. Jeremy.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I have to clarify something with the witness from this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Then put it on the screen and then we'll see it. And the -- already there's no objections against it to be admitted. Madam Registrar, you have identified the document, 65 ter 05751.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: That's it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Which page do you need, Mr. Lukic?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: First -- first page to see the -- so the witness can see the first page and familiarise himself with the first page. And then we need the second page. Can we see the second page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In this ultimatum, it is stated --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'll read it in English so -- then I can ask the question. "The Bosnian Serb army resumed attacks against the Srebrenica enclave on Friday, 7th July 1995. Firing indiscriminately into the safe area and directly targeting UN facilities causing several civilian deaths."

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Which date is this? When was it hit? Was the 7th? The 8th? The 9th? Or the 10th of July? And did, on any of these days, a shell ever fall on the DutchBat compound?

utterances.speaker: EVERT RAVE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think you refer now to the shell that fell on the compound on the Bravo Company on the 11th. I'm not aware of other shells in advance of that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But, Mr. Lukic, it says "targeting UN facilities" and not limited to the compound. Are you aware of any -- any facilities having been target on Friday, the 7th of July or any earlier? UN facilities.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Earlier, for sure, of course, because the attack on OP Echo started in -- earlier than the 7th, I think. And after that, also OP Foxtrot was attacked, and I think it started on the 7th of July with the attack on OP Foxtrot when a Serbian tank fired on the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Mladic should remain seated.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When the Serbian tank fired on OP Foxtrot, I think it was on the 7th.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So there has been -- Mr. Lukic, I'm trying to follow the text of what it is. Yes, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you know that the death of any civilian had been caused during any one of these attacks or situations when fire was opened at UN facilities, as is stated here?

utterances.speaker: EVERT RAVE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what the target was, but I know in those periods -- or in this period several civilians were killed. And I don't know if they were killed while they were in the vicinity of a UN facility or somewhere else, and I don't know what the aim of the shooting was and what the target was.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you know where this information came from? The information that is included in this ultimatum.

utterances.speaker: EVERT RAVE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Just this. Do you know -- this is a document of the 9th of July, 1995, as I see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please just see the first page of this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: This is my question: Can you tell us what the date of this document is? Is the document itself dated the 9th of July, 1995?

utterances.speaker: EVERT RAVE [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can see, it's -- it's the 9th of July, 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We have information that throughout this period in Srebrenica, only one civilian passed away. Do you have different information? Is there more than one civilian fatality throughout that period?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] Throughout which period, Mr. Lukic?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What's your period, Mr. Lukic?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: As of 2nd of July, 1995.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Last week -- one week before the 9th.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: One week before till the 13th.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You said that in this period several civilians died. What period did you have in mind?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I should have a look in my diary, because I think in my diaries, I got some information about shellings and casualties.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Before you consult your diaries -- no problem, Mr. Lukic?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We don't have any problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No problem, Mr. Jeremy?

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please. You -- you may consult your diary.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I've got here in my diary on the 7th of July, in the morning, some artillery fire results some casualties, civilians, in Potocari and Srebrenica and possible death. In Srebrenica yesterday, so the 6th of July, in the centre, a grenade. For sure, one death and seven wounded. So ... I don't have to go through it all, but ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, depends. Mr. Lukic, apparently the witness his recollection is based on and can be confirmed to some extent by what he wrote at the time. I don't know whether you want to further pursue the matter or whether you want to move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I think that we have confirmed one death from these note the as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And one possible death. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: But not confirmed, as I understood.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I leave it to you whether you want -- of course, the witness could go back in his diary and see whether there are more. If you insist, but, at the same time ...

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We will -- actually, just ask one more question.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What are your sources of information concerning that? Namely, that civilians were injured and that there is the possibility of certain deaths. What is your source of information?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: There's one dead and one possible death, Mr. Lukic. We should quote the witness in accordance with his testimony.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: About the victims of shelling, I don't know what the sources were, specifically in this case, but the sources I usually had when I wrote this down was either from the MSF, either from the UNMOs or from the Dutch battalion.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Including personal observation.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No personal observation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now I'd just like to ask you something very briefly about Naser Oric. You know who he is, don't you?

utterances.speaker: EVERT RAVE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you know when and how Naser Oric left Srebrenica? Also, do you know whether that was done with UN assistance?

utterances.speaker: EVERT RAVE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Starting with part number 3 of your question, it was not done with UN assistance. I think that last time we spoke to him was in March, and I have to check in my diary, because, after that, we dealt with Mr. Becirovic, Ramiz. So from March or the beginning of April, he disappeared from the enclave and I don't know how.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Mladic should remain seated. And should speak not aloud.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We have the book of Srebrenica stills. And on the insistence of my client, I will show one photograph to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I don't know the name -- the number of the exhibit. It's trial video Srebrenica stills.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Which is number ...?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It should be P1148, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And perhaps, Mr. McCloskey could assist you. What is the picture you would like to put to this witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Since I didn't prepare this one --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I do understand but if you say what it --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: It's page 41 in the book. I don't know in e-court, probably --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Most likely some 10 or 12 pages further.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Your Honours, I think it's e-court page 53.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: 53. But ... 1148 is -- isn't that the video? No. It's -- okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: That's -- that's the picture I'm looking for.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then ask your question, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We see here that what is stated is that it's the town of Srebrenica, the 12th of July, 1995, and what is documented is a body in the street. Probably in Srebrenica. Do you have any information about this man? And do you know where he lost his life and what his name was?

utterances.speaker: EVERT RAVE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: That was my question --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, no further questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: No further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Jeremy, could you give us an indication as to how much time you'd need.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Less than 15 minutes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Less than 15 minutes. Is that ten or five? Both are less than 15 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: I would say between 10 and 15 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Between 10 and 15 minutes. Then I suggest that we take the break first. Then you have 10 to 15 minutes and then there is close to half an hour left for the next witness to come and start his testimony. We'd like to see you back after the break. As you may have understood, we'll conclude your testimony today, Mr. Rave. You may follow the usher.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We take a break, and we resume at 25 minutes to 2.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could the witness be escorted into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Rave, you'll now be re-examined by Mr. Jeremy. Mr. Jeremy, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. Could we please call to the screen 65 ter 05751. That's the ultimatum document we were discussing just before the break.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Mr. Rave, on page 1 of this document, the following is written: "Attached is the final version of the warning to the Bosnian Serbs. We have sent it as a CAP SAT to General Mladic and we will issue it as a press statement." My question for you is: What is a CAP SAT?

utterances.speaker: EVERT RAVE [Resumed]
utterances.text: A CAP SAT is a communication via the satellite, so that was the only communication over bigger distances to use.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And, Your Honours, I tender that document now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 05751 receives number P1152, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Maybe I can add something we had before about the ultimatum. We were speaking about the ultimatum and targeting UN facilities. I looked in my diary and found out that on the 6th of July, three tank rounds were fired on the OP Foxtrot, so in advance of the date of the 7th. And also on the 6th of July, rockets, artillery and mortar grenades were fired into the enclave, and I found by myself a 14-year-old boy who was wounded in the vicinity of Potocari. And at that same moment, they told me that a 15-year-old girl was died. So I didn't see it myself but that is information from the local population.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed, Mr. Jeremy.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Mr. Rave, during cross-examination yesterday at T -- transcript page 10204 and 10217, and also again today at transcript page 41 and 50, you spoke about the -- the fall or the -- and the takeover of OP Echo. In a sentence or two, could you describe what you are referring to by the fall or the takeover of OP Echo?

utterances.speaker: EVERT RAVE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, OP Echo was attacked in advance in the end of the May. Colonel Vukovic and Major Nikolic talked to us because they wanted to use the road on which OP Echo was in the southern part of the enclave. And I don't know the exact date, but at a certain moment, I think about more than 100 VRS soldiers attacked the OP with several types of weapons, kicked out the manning of the OP and took it over.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would ask the Court Officer to please bring up 65 ter 05696.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And while this is being brought up, this is a Drina Corps order dated the 2nd of June, 1995, to the command of the Bratunac Brigade and the commander of the Manoeuvre Battalion of the Drina Corps relating to the taking control of Zeleni Jadar area. It's signed by Major-General Milenko Zivanovic. Mr. Rave, in paragraph 1 of the document, there's an order to the battalion's deputy commander to "ensure full combat readiness towards enemy and toward UNPROFOR check-point by 0500 on the 3rd of June." Halfway down the second page in the English version, we see an order for Legenda's soldiers to carefully approach the UNPROFOR location. That's ... the quote goes on to say: "This is the moment in which UNPROFOR is expected to surrender. If the UNPROFOR continue threatening to use weapons towards Legenda, use a Zolja to neutralise a personnel carrier." It further goes on to say: "Legenda and Petrovic shall take control of the UNPROFOR check-point." Mr. Rave, are you aware of which UNPROFOR check-points this order is referring to?

utterances.speaker: EVERT RAVE [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I see this and I see the time schedule, the -- should be OP Echo.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And are you aware of what a Zolja is?

utterances.speaker: EVERT RAVE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. But when they want to neutralise a personnel carrier, I think it's in -- RPG, rocket-propelled grenade, was one of things that is able to neutralise an APC.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And, Your Honours, I tender that document as the next Prosecution exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No objections. Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 05696 receives number P1153, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Mr. Rave, in relation to the same topic, I'd like to show you another document and this is the Dutch debriefing document that we saw yesterday, 65 ter 17353.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: If we can go to page 16 in the -- in e-court in English and 21 in the B/C/S. That's paragraph 2.47 on page 15 of the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And from the third line onwards this reads as follows: "On the 3rd of June, OP E was attacked by the BSA using handheld weapons, mortars and anti-tank weapons. OP E was surrendered and two new OP Es (OP S and OP U) were immediately set up to take over the task of OP E. From then onwards, DutchBat were no longer able to disarm BiH soldiers, as there was ultimately no co-operation whatsoever from the local authorities (including the local civilian [sic] police)." Mr. Rave, does the paragraph that I have read out comport with your recollection of events?

utterances.speaker: EVERT RAVE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And was this attack on a DutchBat observation post part of an isolated incident or was it part of a pattern of attacks by the VRS?

utterances.speaker: EVERT RAVE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think from that moment on the attack on the enclave started. It was a try-out what the reactions from UNPROFOR would be, because in advance of this attack they asked us to surrender and to hand over the OP, at least the location. We told them at that moment that we wouldn't do that, and eventually asked for close air support when the OP was attacked. Well, at the end, they attacked the OP. I think we asked for close air support but nothing happened. So they had the confirmation, in my opinion, what they wanted.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And, Your Honours, in relation to this debriefing document, it's clear that it's been used by Defence and Prosecution so there are a number of relevant sections. It is, however, 101 pages long, so I don't propose tendering that now, but my intention is to discuss the document with Mr. Lukic and the Defence and come to agreement on what paragraphs in that document we would tender to the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Until now, I think quotes were always given, so we have a full record at this moment. But if the parties can agree on a selection to be tendered, then the Chamber is waiting to see the result of your conversations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: If I may just ask for clarification on this page. Mr. Rave, third line from the bottom of that page, it says: "Able to disarm BiH soldiers ..." Are you able to tell us what BiH soldiers mean here? Is it Bosnian Serbs or the ABiH?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The ABiH soldiers in the enclave. At least at that moment, some of them in uniforms, others in civilian clothes, who acted as the Bosnian Muslims who defended the enclave.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Mr. Rave, moving to my last question --

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Can I ask that P793 be brought to our screens. This is a -- this document is a DutchBat report from Srebrenica. I'd like to go to page 4 of that document in the original and in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Mr. Rave, if I can draw your attention to the middle of the page, where it says: "Srebrenica update: DTG1131100B, July 1995." Can you interpret the date and time for us of that?

utterances.speaker: EVERT RAVE [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's the 13th of July, 11.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And can we next go to page 5 of that document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Jeremy, I think it's now the 10th or the 15th time that we ask witnesses to explain what the date, time, group is. That is -- everyone in this courtroom should now be aware of it and we can avoid it for the future.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And, Your Honours, I should take this opportunity to note that this question relates to the Bandera triangle which was discussed with this witness today at temporary transcript page 55, cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Of course, now I did stop -- well, I didn't stop Mr. Lukic, but I very much encouraged him only to explore new matters. If it is a matter which, as Mr. McCloskey told us, is not in dispute, then we should refrain from responding to what Mr. Lukic left out.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: The question is in a different category, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Different category, okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Mr. Rave, if I can refer your attention to page 5 and I'd like to draw your attention to the particular passage which states: "The number of BiH soldiers that are taken POW by the Bosnian Serb Army is not known yet, but General Mladic told the UNMO team and the CO DutchBat that the BiH have several hundred dead soldiers in the area of the Bandera triangle." My question is: Apart from this statement from General Mladic, were you aware of any information from your DutchBat sources that there were several hundred dead BiH soldiers in the area of the Bandera triangle?

utterances.speaker: EVERT RAVE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not from sources within the -- the battalion, but General Mladic himself told me that in the north-western part and not only inside the enclave but also outside the enclave, lots of Muslims were killed and we had to stop this because also a lot of VRS soldiers were killed. So that's the only information I've got now.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And thank you, Your Honours. I've no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Jeremy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Since the Bench has no questions, questions in re-examination have not triggered any -- have not triggered any further questions by the Defence. Mr. -- one second, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Mladic is supposed to be seated now. Mr. Rave, we -- first of all, I'd like to thank you very much for coming and having answered all the questions that were put to you by the parties and by the Bench. This concludes your testimony. I wish you a safe return home again. But before doing so, we received a message through the Victims and Witness Section. We'll pay proper attention to that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You -- you may follow the usher.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before I invite the Prosecution to call its next witness, Mr. Lukic, through VWS, the Chamber has received information about inappropriate gestures made by the accused to this witness. We'll verify that. We have an opportunity to do so. But just, it was relatively at the end of the previous session. We preferred first to conclude the testimony of the witness and then to find out what the gestures were and to verify whether the witness described them accurately. And the Chamber will consider whether any consequences will be attached to it. I leave it to that at this moment. Is the Prosecution ready to call its next witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey -- could the -- the witness may be escorted into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Jeremy.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Your Honours, may I be excused?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You are excused, Mr. Jeremy. Mr. McCloskey, no protective measures; 92 ter?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Van Duijn. Before you give evidence, the Rules require that you make a solemn declaration. May I invite you to make that solemn declaration of which the text is now handed out to you by the usher.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Van Duijn. Please be seated. Mr. Van Duijn, we have only 20 minutes left today and we'll continue tomorrow but we didn't want to lose any time. Therefore you will now be first examined by Mr. McCloskey. Mr. McCloskey is counsel for the Prosecution. Mr. McCloskey, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT VAN DUIJN
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Could you please state your full name and your current position or title.

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT VAN DUIJN
utterances.text: My name is Leendert Van Duijn. I'm actually now a commissioner of the police, the Dutch national police.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And have you had a chance to review your testimony from the Popovic trial of 27 to 29 September, 2006?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT VAN DUIJN
utterances.text: Yes, I've had the opportunity, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And if you were asked the same questions that you were asked then, would your answers be substantially the same?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT VAN DUIJN
utterances.text: Yes, they would be the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And did you provide that -- that testimony, was it true and correct?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT VAN DUIJN
utterances.text: It was true and correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, I have the reduced excerpts of that transcript, the 46 pages that I would like to offer into evidence - it's 28794 - along with the associated exhibits that are noted in the filing.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: No new objections beyond that which was in the Rule 92 ter response that was filed by the Defence, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey, one of the reasons why the Chamber prefers not transcript testimonies but rather statements is because they're usually very lengthy. This one is relatively limited excerpts. That doesn't mean that our guidance is not still valid and I said something about it recently. Please take that seriously, but, at this moment, we'll admit into evidence the transcript under Rule 92 ter. Madam Registrar, the number would be ...?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 28794 receives number P1154, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P1154 is admitted into evidence. Associated exhibits, Mr. McCloskey, are ...?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, they -- they --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Were they not reduced in number?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: They were noted as 65 ter number 05177. It was -- and 153584, a few important photographs and an aerial image which are noted in the -- on the filing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Any objections?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 05177 receives number P1155, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: And document 13584 receives number P1156, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Also admitted into evidence. Please proceed, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And if I may, I'll read a short summary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You've explained to the witness the purpose of it?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]. You talked of an aerial image. I see it's a separate 65 ter number. Aren't you tendering that one? 13750?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: The number of the aerial image should be 13584.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I beg your pardon. It's duplicated. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: From sometime in January through the 21st of July, 1995, Leen Van Duijn was a first lieutenant and platoon commander in the Royal Dutch Army and a member of the DutchBat contingent of the United Nations Protection Force assigned to the Srebrenica enclave. The witness described the restrictions of the supply convoys to the Srebrenica enclave imposed by the VRS and explained how this affected DutchBat's ability to do their job and protect the enclave. On 9 and 10 July, he was ordered to take two APCs and set up blocking positions in the south of the enclave, in order to block the VRS advance on the enclave. While taking up various positions along the road, his APCs were targeted by the VRS numerous times, forcing him to move steadily back towards the town of Srebrenica. On 11 July, he withdrew to the UN base in Srebrenica and was eventually ordered to withdraw back to the UN base in Potocari. On 12 and 13 July, he was assigned to the Potocari area where he was in charge of assisting the thousands of Muslim refugees who had gathered there. During this time, he witnessed the separations of men and boys from their families and spoke with various Serb officers working there at that time. He also spoke to and was spoken by -- or spoken to General Mladic. All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: We all know you were --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: This concludes your summary.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, that's it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And now you want to ask him additional questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Just that it's clear on the record where we are. We're now hearing the evidence, whereas you earlier summarised the 92 ter statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you for doing that. I forgot that step. All right. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: It's -- it's clear now that you were a first lieutenant at DutchBat. Can you briefly tell us, well, when you left the army and what your position now -- what it now involves.

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT VAN DUIJN
utterances.text: In 2000 I changed over within the armed forces, over to the Dutch Royal Military Police, Royal Marechaussee, as it is called in the Netherlands. And from 2008 on, I changed over to the Dutch police which is now called the Dutch national police.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And what is your current job and job responsibilities?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters would like to ask the witness to switch on and off the microphone whenever he speaks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Van Duijn, we have a technical problem. Could you switch off your microphone when you're not speaking because it gives additional noise, and technicians are working on it but have not resolved it yet. So therefore could you switch off, if you do not speak, and switch it on again.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'll do that, Your Honour. Currently, I am now a commissioner of police in the Dutch national police. I'm the national programme manager when it comes to the fight against trafficking and smuggling of human beings. I do that with the responsibility to coordinate and collaborate within police units, expertise, intelligence and criminal investigations, but also with local authorities and, for instance, victim assistance organisations. I work for the deputy chief of police of the Dutch national police.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. I won't spend a lot of time with you. I just want to have you clarify a couple of points. We heard about the blocking positions. Can you briefly describe what that job was and what happened? Just briefly. The --

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT VAN DUIJN
utterances.text: I was sent to take up the blocking positions south of the town of Srebrenica. Actually, as the -- it was called blocking position, tried to block the Serb forces that were threatening the -- the city and basically the whole area. We stood there with more APCs than only my two APCs and basically tried to stop the advancement of the Serb forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Do you recall the first date that you and this group of APCs did that?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT VAN DUIJN
utterances.text: On the evening of the 9th, basically the first day that the shelling started. On that evening, late in the evening, I moved up with from APCs from Potocari base to Srebrenica base to help and assist the Bravo Company that was responsible for the south of the enclave.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And what did you do to try to stop that advance?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT VAN DUIJN
utterances.text: We took up positions south of the -- of the town, overseeing the town that was in our backs, and -- and the south, basically also the -- the big roads, the one -- only one asphalted road in the enclave, and we tried to stop the advancements by also shooting at the Serb forces that were advancing and trying to stop them advancing. So we were shooting and we were shot at in that position.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And when you say you were shooting, what kind of weaponry did you use to target the Serb forces?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT VAN DUIJN
utterances.text: We only had small-calibre rifles and, on top of our APCs, a heavy machine-gun.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And tell us what happened when you took up these positions and engaged the Serb forces like this.

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT VAN DUIJN
utterances.text: From the start, we -- we took up the positions we were shelled, and -- and the shelling was on our positions but also at the town, so basically with intervals of one hour. That changed over to shelling the town to shelling our positions, and then changed over to the town again, and that lasted for one or two days that we were in the blocking positions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: When you took the blocking positions, did you open up fire on the Serb forces prior to being shelled?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT VAN DUIJN
utterances.text: No, the shelling was starting right away, basically from the 9th on, when I was still at Potocari. So the shelling started the evening of the 9th, and when I arrived at the location of the blocking positions, which changed slightly during the days of the 9th and the 10th, the shelling was constantly going on. So the answer is no.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: In your direction, while you're at the blocking position?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT VAN DUIJN
utterances.text: Yes, in our direction, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Were you able to make out what kind of shells, what kind of rounds were targeting your blocking position?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT VAN DUIJN
utterances.text: From the military intelligence that we had, we knew there were some 155-calibre artillery pieces stationed from the Serb army. So I don't know for sure, but those were big calibre artillery fire shells.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Did you ever -- were you ever targeted by tanks that you could -- as far as you know?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT VAN DUIJN
utterances.text: Not directly.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And how long did you stay at that first blocking position and what ...

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT VAN DUIJN
utterances.text: As I remember correctly, we moved there in the night of the 9th, so we stayed at the first location during the 10th. We drew -- we took up another position that was, I think, 200 metres from the first one also during the -- the 10th.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And why did you withdraw from the first one?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT VAN DUIJN
utterances.text: The area we were in at the evening of the 9th, there were still some refugees and civilians there, and during the day-time of the 10th, the -- the area was basically clear of civilians. And there was a -- a choice made by the Bravo Company commander, Captain Groen that we should take up another position nearer to the asphalted road.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey, could I seek clarification of one of the previous answers. You were asked whether you were ever targeted by tanks, as far as you knew. Your answer was: "Not directly."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Which is ambiguous for me. What do you mean by "not directly"? That you have no first-hand knowledge or ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We knew that there were Serb tanks in the area and Serb tanks have directly attacked other Dutch units. Also the units involved in the forward air controlling of the air support.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, so --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: So -- but not on my position. So I knew that there were tanks in the area and we have seen tanks in the area but they didn't attack us or my position directly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It is mainly an explanation of what the "you" means here. Not you personally but other -- yes, please proceed, Mr. McCloskey, for another two minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And were there Muslim forces around your blocking positions at any -- at any time during this period?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT VAN DUIJN
utterances.text: At the beginning there were, on and off. Sometimes also shooting next to our location also in the direction of the Serb forces advancing, but somewhere along the 10th, also the Muslim forces were -- were withdrawn. So -- in the end of the -- I think the 10th or the 11th, there were no Muslim forces there anymore.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And after the Muslim forces vacated your area, were you ever targeted by the Serb forces, your APCs and people?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT VAN DUIJN
utterances.text: The shelling never stopped. From the 9th on, the shelling commenced. So also when refugees or civilians or Muslim forces were not anymore in the -- in the neighbourhood, the shelling still went on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And how close did these shells get to your APCs?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT VAN DUIJN
utterances.text: Sometimes within the reach of 50 to 100 metres of my APC. So that -- even the dirt of the explosions came onto the APCs.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, I think it's a good time to stop.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. McCloskey. Mr. Van Duijn, we'll conclude for the day. We'd like to see you back tomorrow morning at half past 9.00 in this same courtroom. But before you leave, I want to instruct you that you should not speak or communicate in whatever way with whomever about your testimony, whether that is testimony you've given today, or whether that's testimony you are expected to give tomorrow. Is that clear to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's clear, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then you may follow the usher.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We adjourn for the day, and we'll resume tomorrow, Thursday, the 25th of April, at 9.30 in the morning, in this same courtroom, I.
